Processes and Resource Management

1. Processes and Resource Management

A server feels slow, and the first visible process uses a large amount of memory. Killing it seems decisive, but the process may be the database doing legitimate work while the real problem is a saturated storage path. Resource management requires identifying what is running, what it is waiting for, and which limit actually constrains the workload.

This chapter distinguishes process identity, scheduling, memory accounting, signals, and resource boundaries. Observation comes before termination. A process is part of a service lifecycle, not merely a row to remove from a screen.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — Chapter 7 — Processes and Resource Management

2. Connect workload to constrained resources

A busy CPU is an observation. Compare demand, run queue, memory pressure and service latency before choosing a repair. An arbitrary kill hides the symptom and destroys the evidence needed to explain it.

SOURCE: Connect workload to constrained resources

3. Chapter 7 — Processes and Resource Management

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — Chapter 7 — Processes and Resource Management

4. 7.1 Programs vs. Processes

A program is executable code stored or otherwise available for execution. A process is a running instance with its own identity, address space, open file descriptors, credentials, and execution state. Many processes can run the same program with different arguments and permissions.

A service may consist of one process, a parent and several workers, or a collection of cooperating programs. Killing one worker may cause the supervisor to replace it immediately. That is not evidence that kill failed; it may be the intended lifecycle policy.

Identify the owning service before acting. The service manager often knows which processes belong together and how to stop them cleanly. Stopping a service through its supervisor is usually safer than guessing which PID represents the whole application.

Linux example — 7.1

Compare the executable name with a running instance.

What to check: The file is a program; the shell PID identifies a process executing it.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.1 Programs vs. Processes

6. 7.2 Process IDs

A process ID, or PID, identifies a process within a PID namespace. PIDs are reused after processes exit. A number copied from an old incident note is therefore not a durable identity.

$$ expands to the shell’s PID in the usual interactive context. The elapsed time and command help establish which process is actually being inspected.

Before signaling a process, confirm its current executable, owner, start time, and relationship to the service. A separate check followed by a later signal still has a race if the process exits and the PID is reused. Service-manager operations and newer process-handle interfaces can reduce ambiguity. Avoid building critical automation around stale PID files alone.

Linux example — 7.2

Inspect the current process ID.

What to check: A PID identifies an instance and can be reused after that instance exits.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.2 Process IDs

9. 7.3 Parent and Child Processes

A process can create child processes. The parent PID, or PPID, records a relationship useful for understanding shells, workers, and supervisors. A child can outlive its original parent and be adopted by an appropriate reaper or subreaper.

The process tree reveals relationships, but it does not by itself describe every service boundary. A service’s control group can include processes whose ancestry has changed.

After a child exits, its parent ordinarily collects its termination status through a wait operation. Failing to do so creates a zombie entry, discussed later. Good process supervision includes starting, signaling, collecting exit status, and deciding whether restart is appropriate.

Linux example — 7.3

Observe a controlled child process.

What to check: The child should show your shell as its parent; wait reaps its completion.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.3 Parent and Child Processes

12. 7.4 ps

ps reports a snapshot of selected processes. Its option styles have historical differences, so use an explicit format when collecting repeatable evidence.

The command sorts by the reported CPU measure and avoids dumping complete arguments that might contain secrets. Add arguments only when needed and handle them as potentially sensitive.

ps CPU percentages are not necessarily the same interval measurement shown by an interactive monitor. Its values often reflect CPU time relative to process lifetime. A recently busy process and a long-running process can therefore look different depending on the tool’s measurement model. State the tool and observation interval when reporting performance. (R14)

Linux example — 7.4

Select useful process columns.

What to check: This is a snapshot, not an interval measurement.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.4 ps

15. 7.5 top and htop

top repeatedly samples processes and system activity. htop, when installed, offers a different interactive interface with convenient navigation. Both are views of measurements, not automatic diagnoses.

Check whether CPU percentages are normalized per logical CPU or across the whole machine. A multithreaded process can exceed 100% in a per-CPU reporting mode. Use thread views when one process contains several independently busy threads.

For a bounded noninteractive sample:

The first display may have different averaging semantics from subsequent interval displays. Avoid drawing a conclusion from one frame. Correlate CPU, memory, runnable tasks, and I/O with application latency and throughput. (R15)

Linux example — 7.5

Take one bounded top snapshot.

What to check: top's display and CPU accounting depend on its sampling interval.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.5 top and htop

18. 7.6 Foreground and Background Jobs

A foreground job interacts with the terminal normally. Appending & starts a command asynchronously and returns the shell prompt. Bash assigns a job number distinct from the operating-system PID.

$! captures the PID associated with the most recent asynchronous command. fg returns a job to the foreground; bg resumes a stopped job in the background. These are shell job-control operations, not service-management commands.

Backgrounding a command does not make it a reliable daemon. It may depend on the session, terminal, environment, or working directory. Use a terminal multiplexer for interactive continuity and a supervisor such as systemd for an actual service with restart and logging requirements.

Linux example — 7.6

Run and wait for a short background job.

What to check: jobs reports this shell's job table, not every host process.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.6 Foreground and Background Jobs

21. 7.7 Signals

A signal notifies a process of an event or requests an action. SIGTERM asks for termination and can be handled for cleanup. SIGINT commonly corresponds to an interactive interrupt. SIGHUP has historical terminal meaning and application-specific uses. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored.

Do not assume that SIGHUP always reloads configuration. That is an application convention, not a universal kernel rule. Read the service documentation or use its supported reload interface.

SIGKILL prevents application cleanup and can leave incomplete work. It is a last resort after understanding the impact. It also does not make an uninterruptible kernel wait vanish immediately; delivery takes effect when the process can reach an appropriate point.

Linux example — 7.7

List supported signal names.

What to check: TERM allows a program to handle termination; KILL cannot be caught.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.7 Signals

23. 7.8 kill and pkill

kill sends a signal; its name does not mean every use immediately destroys a process. pkill selects processes by criteria and signals the matches. Selection deserves at least as much care as the signal itself.

Inspect a proposed match with pgrep before using a corresponding pkill. Exact-name matching is safer than a broad substring, but still may match multiple legitimate jobs. Never run pkill -f against an unreviewed pattern on a production host.

For the known lab process started in Section 7.6, kill -TERM "$job_pid" targets the captured child. Wait for its completion in the same shell with wait "$job_pid", interpreting the expected signal-related status. Do not reuse the variable later after unrelated work.

Linux example — 7.8

Terminate only the sleep process created here.

What to check: wait commonly reports a signal-related nonzero status; avoid broad pkill patterns.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.8 kill and pkill

26. 7.9 Process Priorities

Scheduling priority influences how runnable work competes for CPU time. It does not manufacture CPU capacity and does not resolve every performance problem. A process blocked on storage may gain little from a CPU-priority change.

Ordinary Linux scheduling and real-time scheduling have different policies. Raising a process into a real-time class without understanding its behavior can starve important system work. Do not treat real-time priority as a generic performance switch.

Measure the actual bottleneck first. For background maintenance, reducing scheduling preference may be appropriate when it protects interactive service latency. Even then, the job can still compete for memory and I/O, so CPU priority is only one part of resource control.

Linux example — 7.9

Inspect scheduling priority fields.

What to check: NI is the nice adjustment; it is not a CPU quota.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.9 Process Priorities

28. 7.10 nice and renice

nice starts a command with an adjusted niceness; renice changes an existing process’s niceness. In the ordinary range, a larger numeric nice value means lower scheduling preference. Negative values increase preference and ordinarily require privilege.

The small example demonstrates syntax without creating a sustained load. For an existing identified process, inspect its current value before changing it with renice.

Niceness is relative competition, not a hard CPU ceiling. A low-priority job can use an otherwise idle CPU fully. For a service that must not exceed a defined allocation, a control-group quota or another explicit resource limit may be more appropriate.

Linux example — 7.10

Start a low-priority disposable process.

What to check: The child normally shows NI 10 when the parent started at NI 0.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.10 nice and renice

31. 7.11 CPU Utilization

CPU utilization describes how processor time is being spent. Distinguish user-space work, kernel work, idle time, and other reported categories. A busy CPU can indicate productive work, an inefficient loop, encryption, interrupt load, or many other causes.

A machine with eight logical CPUs can have one saturated application thread while the overall CPU average remains modest. Conversely, a high aggregate percentage can be acceptable when latency targets are met and the workload is intentionally batch-oriented.

Use interval measurements and thread-level evidence when appropriate. Compare against the service’s throughput and response time. “CPU is 100%” is incomplete until you state which CPU or process, over what interval, and whether useful work is progressing.

Linux example — 7.11

Sample CPU scheduling and runnable work.

What to check: Ignore the first cumulative report when comparing the two later interval samples.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.11 CPU Utilization

33. 7.12 Memory Utilization

Linux uses memory for application pages, kernel data, page cache, and other purposes. A low free value is not automatically a problem because cache can often be reclaimed. The available estimate is more useful for understanding memory that can likely support new work without swapping.

Process RSS is resident memory, while VSZ describes virtual address space. Large virtual size does not mean every byte is physically resident. Summing RSS can also double-count shared pages across processes.

Investigate growth over time, reclaim activity, swap traffic, allocation failures, and cgroup limits. A memory leak is a pattern tied to workload and lifetime, not simply the largest process in one snapshot. Chapter 22 develops a more complete measurement sequence.

Linux example — 7.12

Inspect memory accounting.

What to check: Available memory is a better starting point than treating all cache as unavailable.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.12 Memory Utilization

35. 7.13 Load Average

Linux load averages summarize the number of runnable tasks and tasks in certain uninterruptible waits over approximately one, five, and fifteen minutes. They are not CPU percentages.

A load of four means different things on a one-CPU machine and a sixteen-CPU machine. High load with idle CPU can point toward blocked I/O or other uninterruptible waits rather than a shortage of computation.

Compare the trend across intervals: a short-term value much higher than the long-term value suggests a recent increase. Then inspect task states and resource evidence. Dividing load by CPU count can provide context, but it does not turn the result into a universal health score.

Linux example — 7.13

Compare load with CPU count.

What to check: Load includes runnable and uninterruptible tasks, so it is not the same as CPU utilization.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.13 Load Average

37. 7.14 Zombie Processes

A zombie is a process that has exited but whose termination status has not yet been collected by its parent. It is not continuing to execute application code or holding its former full address space.

Sending SIGKILL to a zombie does not solve the underlying problem because it has already exited. Investigate the parent and why it is not reaping children. A small transient number may be normal; a growing accumulation suggests a supervision or application defect.

Restarting a parent can be disruptive and should follow the service’s recovery procedure. Record the process relationship and growth pattern before acting. The visible zombie is evidence of a lifecycle problem, not an independent runaway workload.

Linux example — 7.14

Find zombie states without creating zombies deliberately.

What to check: Look for Z in STAT; investigate the parent that has not reaped the child.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.14 Zombie Processes

39. 7.15 Out-of-Memory Conditions

When memory cannot be supplied under the relevant constraints, the kernel or a userspace memory-pressure manager may terminate processes. A cgroup can encounter an out-of-memory condition even when the host still has free memory outside that group’s limit.

Inspect kernel logs, service logs, and cgroup memory events. Do not infer a global memory shortage solely from a service disappearing. Exit status, signal information, and recorded OOM evidence help distinguish causes.

Adding swap may provide breathing room for some workloads but can also introduce unacceptable latency. Increasing a limit without understanding growth can delay the same failure. The corrective action may be reducing concurrency, fixing a leak, changing caching behavior, or increasing capacity based on measured demand.

Linux example — 7.15

Search for OOM evidence on a systemd host.

What to check: Find OOM and killed-process messages; distinguish kernel OOM from a userspace memory manager.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.15 Out-of-Memory Conditions

40. 7.15 Out-of-Memory Conditions · example 1

When memory cannot be supplied under the relevant constraints, the kernel or a userspace memory-pressure manager may terminate processes. A cgroup can encounter an out-of-memory condition even when the host still has free memory outside that group’s limit.

Inspect kernel logs, service logs, and cgroup memory events. Do not infer a global memory shortage solely from a service disappearing. Exit status, signal information, and recorded OOM evidence help distinguish causes.

Adding swap may provide breathing room for some workloads but can also introduce unacceptable latency. Increasing a limit without understanding growth can delay the same failure. The corrective action may be reducing concurrency, fixing a leak, changing caching behavior, or increasing capacity based on measured demand.

Linux example — 7.15

Search for OOM evidence on a systemd host.

What to check: Find OOM and killed-process messages; distinguish kernel OOM from a userspace memory manager.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.15 Out-of-Memory Conditions

41. 7.16 Resource Limits

Per-process resource limits constrain resources such as open file descriptors, core-file size, and process creation. ulimit is a shell interface to selected limits. A soft limit is the active boundary; a hard limit constrains how far the soft limit may be raised without additional privilege.

Changing a login shell’s limit does not automatically change an already-running systemd service. Configure the relevant service’s LimitNOFILE= or other supported setting, then restart and inspect its effective limits.

A “too many open files” error can reflect a process limit, a leak, or another system boundary. Raising the limit may be appropriate, but first count descriptors and determine whether the workload closes resources correctly.

Linux example — 7.16

Read the current shell's resource limits.

What to check: Child processes inherit limits; service managers can impose different limits.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.16 Resource Limits

44. 7.17 Control Groups

Control groups, or cgroups, organize processes for resource accounting and control. They can constrain CPU, memory, process counts, and I/O according to available controllers. systemd uses cgroups to group service processes and apply policy.

Cgroup v2 presents a unified hierarchy with controller-specific interfaces. A limit is meaningful only when the relevant controller and hierarchy support it. Do not blindly write values into /sys/fs/cgroup on a system managed by another owner.

Use systemd properties such as MemoryMax=, CPUQuota=, and TasksMax= for managed services when appropriate. A quota limits available CPU time; a weight influences relative competition. Neither is a substitute for understanding workload requirements. Test throttling and failure behavior before applying limits to production. (R16)

Linux example — 7.17

Inspect this process's cgroup placement.

What to check: A cgroup path locates the policy scope; inspect that scope's controls before drawing conclusions.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — 7.17 Control Groups

46. Requirement and simplest approach

HarborWorks wants to observe a background task and stop only that task. Matching every process containing the word sleep is unnecessarily broad. A freshly captured child PID provides a better lab boundary.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — Requirement and simplest approach

47. Command walkthrough

Change — one ordinary-user process. Run in a single Bash session:

The stopped process should show a stopped state, commonly containing T. After SIGCONT, it can run again. The final status is expected to indicate signal termination rather than ordinary successful completion. The exact printed diagnostics can vary by shell settings.

50. Interpretation and recovery

There is no reason to use SIGKILL because sleep responds to termination. The parent shell collects the status with wait. Verify that the identified process is no longer present, but do not treat a later reused PID as the original task.

For a real service, use the service manager to stop the whole managed unit. A PID captured by a script is useful within a controlled lifetime, not a permanent handle suitable for a future maintenance window.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — Interpretation and recovery

51. Practice and implementation lab

Observe a short-lived command and a long-lived service using both ps and top. Explain why their reported CPU percentages may differ. Do not generate unbounded load to make the display interesting.

Read the current shell’s open-file limits and compare them with a chosen systemd service’s effective limits. Identify which configuration would need to change for each context.

Check your understanding. Is load average CPU utilization? No. Does a zombie need to be killed? No; its parent needs to collect its status. Can a service be OOM-killed while the host has spare memory? Yes, when a relevant cgroup or other memory policy constrains it.

Chapter takeaway. Diagnose resource pressure through identity, state, measurement interval, and governing limits before changing priority or terminating work.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch009.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

52. Select resource-heavy process evidence

Sort recorded process samples. These invented measurements are not a live performance diagnosis. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Select resource-heavy process evidence
